title: Bigfoot Is Back on the Big Screen — and This Time He's Bringing Secrets
summary:
Have you ever seen a blurry photo and wondered, 'Is that real?' Imagine a blurry film that people have argued about for almost 60 years.

In 1967, two friends named Roger Patterson and Robert Gimlin went into a forest in Northern California. They said they saw a Bigfoot. Patterson grabbed his camera and filmed 59 seconds of a tall, hairy creature walking through the woods. People named the creature 'Patty.'

That short film became one of the most studied pieces of footage in history. Some people believe it. Some people say it's a fake. Nobody has ever proven it either way.

Now there's a new documentary called 'Capturing Bigfoot.' It premiered earlier this year at a big film festival in Texas, and the crowd went wild. But then the movie disappeared — no one could see it. Why? The filmmakers wanted to keep the surprises secret.

Here's the twist: a reel of old film was found in a safe five decades later. The documentary says this film 'blows the legend wide open.' It includes interviews with people who were there, including Roger's own son, Clint Patterson, who has never talked about it before.

The movie comes out on October 20 — National Bigfoot Day — in select cities and on Prime Video. At theaters, security will be tight. No phones allowed. They really want to protect the mystery.

So... is Bigfoot real? Grab a friend, watch the movie, and decide for yourself.
why_it_matters: Bigfoot's story is a fun reminder to ask 'how do we actually know?' — the same skill you use when a classmate tells you a wild rumor.

background_read: Bigfoot is a legendary giant, hair-covered creature that people claim to have seen in the forests of North America (the continent that includes the United States and Canada).
The most famous 'proof' is the 1967 Patterson-Gimlin film, which scientists and fans have argued about for decades — nobody has ever proven that Bigfoot is real.
Stories about hidden creatures like Bigfoot are sometimes called 'cryptids,' and Scotland's Loch Ness Monster (a huge beast said to live in a lake) is another famous one.
Article_Structure: WHO: Roger Patterson and Robert Gimlin, who filmed the 1967 'Bigfoot' footage, plus Clint Patterson (Roger's son), who speaks about it for the first time in the new documentary.
WHAT: A new documentary called 'Capturing Bigfoot' says a reel of old film found in a safe 'blows the legend wide open.'
WHERE: The original sighting happened in a Northern California forest, the documentary premiered at a film festival in Texas, and it opens in select cities and on Prime Video.
WHY: The filmmakers kept the movie hidden for months to protect the surprises, and theaters will ban phones to keep the mystery safe.

perspectives.description: Fans say the blurry film and the new documentary are real clues that a giant creature lives in the woods, and they are excited that the movie 'blows the legend wide open.'
Others point out that the film is blurry and nobody has ever proven it either way, so they think it is a made-up story rather than science.
They say they hid the movie on purpose and will not allow phones in theaters, because they want audiences to enjoy the surprise without spoilers.
